analysis.one_liner: Bans federal officeholders from personally asking anyone for campaign money.
analysis.headline: The Stop Act, which would bar members of Congress from directly soliciting donations, sat in the House Administration Committee without a markup or vote and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal campaign finance law to prohibit anyone holding federal office from directly asking any person for campaign contributions, whether for their own committee or anyone else's. Members could still plan, attend, speak at, and be featured guests at fundraising events — they just could not personally make the written or verbal ask. It was a narrow rule change aimed at the day-to-day practice in which members of Congress spend hours on 'call time' dialing donors for money.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want members of Congress spending their time on legislating rather than dialing donors, and small donors whose contributions would count for relatively more without the constant personal ask from officeholders. Voters generally, since the practice the bill targets is the one that ties officeholders to the people who fund their campaigns.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits federal officeholders from soliciting campaign funds directly from any person, for any political committee or for federal election activity [S2][S3].

Still allows officeholders to participate in fundraising events — planning, attending, speaking, or serving as a featured guest — as long as they make no written or verbal solicitation of funds [S2][S3].
Takes effect immediately upon enactment, applying to solicitations made on or after that date [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent members of Congress lose a central fundraising tool: the personal ask. Professional fundraisers and campaign consultants who organize members' call time and donor events would see their role change. Major donors lose the direct personal solicitation from the officeholder himself, though they could still give and members could still appear at their events.

drawbacks.text: The bill still lets officeholders headline, attend, and be featured at donor events, so the access donors buy with big checks — and the incentive to court them — remains; it removes the literal ask but not the fundraising structure [S2][S3].

A ban on 'written or verbal solicitation' is difficult to police in practice, since events can be arranged so that staff, hosts, or others make the ask while the officeholder stands by, and enforcement would run through campaign finance regulators whose funding and authority Congress controls [S3].

Critics of solicitation bans generally argue that pressuring donors for contributions is itself protected political speech, so a direct-solicitation prohibition faces plausible constitutional challenge; the bill text does not address this [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The change is real but modest: it strikes at the most time-consuming and most personally compromising part of member fundraising — the call-time ask — while leaving the event circuit and big-donor access intact. It would not remove money from congressional politics; it would remove the officeholder's own voice from the transaction, a meaningful symbol and some practical separation, but not a structural fix.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2016 and sent to the House Committee on House Administration, which never took it up, and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. David Jolly introduced the Stop Act on February 3, 2016, with five additional original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on House Administration the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
Jolly gave introductory remarks on the bill on the House floor twice, on February 24 and March 1, 2016, but no markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever followed [S5].
The bill finished with 9 cosponsors — 5 Republicans and 4 Democrats — a small bipartisan group, and the Congress expired on January 3, 2017 before the committee acted [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress came out ahead: the committee never scheduled action, so every officeholder kept the power to personally solicit donations. Campaign fundraising consultants and the call-time system were untouched, and the bill's own sponsor — Rep. Jolly — had publicly announced he was giving up federal fundraising and would not seek the practice, which drew national attention to the bill's aim but did not move it.

for.name: Rep. David Jolly
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Act and gave two rounds of introductory remarks on the House floor urging its adoption.

for.name: 9 House cosponsors (5 of 246 Republicans, 4 of 188 Democrats)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it small bipartisan support; no Democrat or Republican beyond nine signed on.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in February 2016 and never held a markup, took a vote, or reported the bill out.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Speaker and majority leadership of the 114th House
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote during the remainder of the 114th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but thin: of the 9 cosponsors, 5 were Republicans and 4 were Democrats; no roll-call vote ever occurred, and the bill stalled in a committee controlled by the House Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill strips officeholders of their most personal fundraising tool — the direct ask by phone, in writing, or in person. Inaction left each member free to keep spending hours per day soliciting donors, a practice that shapes whose calls members return. Members of Congress are the regulated party here, and the committee that buried the bill is run by members.

industries.industry: Campaign fundraising consultants and event organizers
industries.note: These professionals build and run the call-time sessions in which members make the personal asks; a ban on direct solicitation would force a rework of that product line. The bill's death left the member-call-time fundraising industry intact.

Big donors would still give and still get the headliner access the bill expressly preserves — members can attend, speak, and be featured guests. The bill's failure preserved a system in which wealthy donors and lobbying interests remain the primary source of campaign funds and the access that follows.
